questions.q: Why does an application need a runtime like @zudojs/runtime?
questions.explain: With two parts, ordering by hand works; at ten it becomes fragile. You describe each part and what it needs, and the runtime works out the order, starts everything, and stops it cleanly.
options: To compile TypeScript to JavaScript before the app starts
To start the parts in dependency order, notice failures, and shut everything down in reverse
To answer HTTP requests faster than Node.js can alone
To store the application's data between restarts

questions.q: What does a runtime module consist of?
questions.explain: The runtime manages modules. Each one says who it is, which other modules it needs (by id), and which hooks the runtime should call at fixed moments.
options: A folder of TypeScript files with an index.ts
An npm package that the runtime installs on start
An object with an id, a name, optional dependencies, and up to four hooks
A class that must extend Error

questions.q: Your store module must open a database connection when the app starts. Which hook is for that?
questions.explain: onInitialize runs during start(), dependencies first: the place to open connections and load data. onReady is for starting to accept work, once every module has initialized.
options: onInitialize
onReady
onShutdown
onDestroy

questions.q: When does the runtime call onReady?
questions.explain: Startup has two rounds: every module is initialized before any becomes ready. So when http becomes ready, every other module has at least been initialized.
options: Right after the same module's onInitialize, before the next module initializes
During start(), after every module has initialized
Only when the first HTTP request arrives
During stop(), before onShutdown

questions.q: What is the difference between onShutdown and onDestroy?
questions.explain: Stopping also has two rounds, both in reverse order: first every onShutdown, then every onDestroy, which releases what the module still holds.
options: onShutdown runs on errors only; onDestroy runs on a normal stop
onShutdown stops accepting work and finishes what runs; onDestroy runs last and releases everything
onShutdown runs in start order; onDestroy runs in reverse order
They are two names for the same hook

questions.q: You register http, then tasks, then store, but store initializes first. Why?
questions.explain: tasks needs store, and http needs tasks. The runtime sorts that dependency graph (a topological sort), so the list order does not matter.
options: The runtime sorts modules by name
The runtime always starts the last module in the list first
The runtime follows the dependencies, not the order of the list
Modules named store are always special

questions.q: A module lists a dependency that is not registered. When does the runtime notice?
questions.explain: The runtime refuses a cycle or a missing dependency before it touches any module. A wiring mistake shows up the first time you start the app, not hours later.
options: When that module's onReady runs
Never; the missing module is skipped
On start(), before any hook runs, because it checks the whole graph first
Only when the first request needs the missing module

questions.q: The runtime says Module "tasks" depends on "databse" which is not registered. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explain: A missing dependency is usually a typo (here databse) or a forgotten registration. It is about the wiring, not about a server being reachable.
options: The database server is down
A typo in the dependencies list, or a module you forgot to register
The modules are listed in the wrong order
The tasks module has no onDestroy hook

questions.q: The http module fails to start because its port is in use, while store and tasks are already up. Why does the runtime roll back?
questions.explain: If the runtime simply gave up, open connections would leak. Rolling back undoes what already happened, in reverse order, before start() rejects.
options: To try starting http again on another port
So what already started, such as the store's connection, is undone in reverse and not left open
To delete the modules that did start
So the app can keep running without http

questions.q: During that rollback, onShutdown ran for tasks and store, but not for http. Why?
questions.explain: Shutdown undoes "ready", so it only runs where ready succeeded. onDestroy ran for all three, because all three had initialized and may hold resources.
options: Because http has no onShutdown hook
Because the runtime forgot it; it is a bug
Only modules that became ready are shut down; http failed in onReady, so it never started
Because http is stopped last, after the process exits

questions.q: A module's onInitialize throws halfway through. The runtime still calls its onDestroy. What does that mean for your code?
questions.explain: The module may have opened something before it threw. So onDestroy runs, and it must check what is actually open instead of assuming a full setup.
options: Nothing; onDestroy can assume everything was set up
onDestroy must cope with a half-initialized module, releasing only what really exists
You must never throw inside onInitialize
You must call onDestroy yourself inside the catch

questions.q: A failed start() rejects with a RuntimeStartError. Where do you find what went wrong?
questions.explain: The RuntimeStartError names the module and the phase. The original error, such as "Port 3000 is already in use", is kept as its cause.
options: Only in the runtime's log file
error.phase says initialize or start, and error.cause holds the original error
error.message holds the original error's stack trace
In runtime.context.lastError

questions.q: In src/server.ts, a failed start should log the error, call runtime.stop(), and exit with code 1. Why code 1?
questions.explain: Exiting with 0 would report success, and nobody would be alerted. Calling stop() first releases anything the rollback did not reach; it is safe to call even when nothing is left.
options: Because code 1 restarts the app automatically
Because Node.js cannot exit with code 0 after an error
A non-zero code tells Docker, systemd or the platform that the app did not start
Because code 1 hides the error from the logs

questions.q: A readiness check for the store starts returning false while the app keeps running. What does the runtime report?
questions.explain: runtime.ready and runtime.health are worked out from all the readiness checks. A platform then sends traffic elsewhere until the app is ready again.
options: It stops the app at once
Not ready, and health degraded: still alive, not fully working
Ready, because the app is still running
Healthy, because only the store is affected

questions.q: What is SIGTERM?
questions.explain: Platforms send SIGTERM; pressing Ctrl + C sends SIGINT. By default Node.js ends the process at once, cutting off requests in progress.
options: An error that Node.js throws when memory runs out
A log level more serious than ERROR
A signal a hosting platform sends to ask your process to stop, for example before a deploy
A network packet that ends an HTTP request

questions.q: What does a graceful shutdown do?
questions.explain: With handleSignals: true the runtime catches the signal and runs stop(). A second signal exits at once, and shutdownTimeout puts an upper limit on the whole thing.
options: Kills the process at once, so the new version starts sooner
Stops accepting new work, finishes work in progress, closes connections, then exits
Ignores the signal until all users have logged out
Restarts the app with the same code

questions.q: Why does the generated src/app.ts pass handleSignals: false?
questions.explain: The HTTP server is not a module. server.ts calls server.stop() (no new requests), then runtime.stop() (close what the requests used). One owner of the signals keeps the order right.
options: Because signals do not exist on Linux servers
Because graceful shutdown is not needed in development
server.ts handles the signals itself, to stop the HTTP server first and then the runtime; two listeners would race
Because the runtime can only handle SIGINT, not SIGTERM

questions.q: What is runtime.context.runtimeId for?
questions.explain: Two copies of task-api may run at once. The id, like rt_…, lets you see which copy wrote which log line.
options: It is the process id that the operating system gave Node.js
It is a secret that authenticates the app to the database
It is new on every run, so you can tell apart two copies of the same app in logs
It is the version number of @zudojs/runtime

questions.q: What does @zudojs/lifecycle add, next to the runtime?
questions.explain: A module may own a pool, a cache and a mailer. Lifecycle starts and stops such components in order, rolls back on failure, and lets a non-critical one fail without stopping startup.
options: A replacement for the runtime that works only in the browser
The same idea one level down: smaller components inside a module, with dependsOn and optional critical: false
A way to write modules without any hooks
A database migration tool

questions.q: TasksModule passes dependencies: ["store"] to BaseModule. What does that guarantee?
questions.explain: Because of the dependency, the store is connected before TasksModule.onInitialize adds its example task. Both modules receive the same TaskStore object.
options: That the store module is created by the tasks module
That the store's onInitialize has run before the tasks module's onInitialize
That the store and tasks modules run in parallel
That the tasks module can never fail

questions.q: Write the heart of the runtime: startOrder(modules) returns the module ids so that every module comes after the modules in its dependencies. Keep the listed order when nothing forces a change.
questions.explain: A topological sort: visit a module's dependencies before adding the module itself, and skip modules already added. http comes before mailer because it was listed first.

questions.q: Finish checkGraph(modules): before starting anything, throw an Error for the first dependency that is not registered, with the message Module "ID" depends on "DEP" which is not registered. Return "ok" when the graph is complete.
questions.explain: Collect the registered ids in a Set, then check every dependency. Doing this before any hook runs is why a wiring mistake never leaves half an app running.
questions.expected:
ok
Module "tasks" depends on "database" which is not registered.

questions.q: Finish findCycle(modules). Follow the dependencies from each module; when you meet a module that is already on the current path, return the loop as text, like tasks -> store -> tasks. Return null if there is no cycle.
questions.explain: Carry the current path along. Meeting an id that is already on the path means a loop; slicing from its first appearance gives exactly the loop, which is what the runtime's error message shows.
questions.expected:
tasks -> store -> tasks
a -> b -> c -> a
null

questions.q: Finish start(ordered): modules are already sorted. Run every onInitialize first, then every onReady, awaiting each one. Hooks are optional.
questions.explain: Two loops give two rounds: when any module becomes ready, every module has already initialized. ?.() skips modules without the hook.
questions.expected:
initialize store
initialize tasks
ready store
ready tasks

questions.q: Finish stop(started): started is in start order. Run every onShutdown in reverse order, then every onDestroy in reverse order. Do not change the started array.
questions.explain: Copy before reversing, because reverse() changes the array in place. Then two loops: all shutdowns, then all destroys, both in reverse start order.
questions.expected:
shutdown http
shutdown tasks
shutdown store
destroy http
destroy tasks
destroy store
store,tasks,http

questions.q: Finish start(ordered) with rollback. Round 1: onInitialize each module and remember it. Round 2: onReady each module and remember it. If any hook throws: run onShutdown for the ready modules in reverse, then onDestroy for the initialized modules in reverse, then rethrow.
questions.explain: A module counts as initialized as soon as its onInitialize begins, because it may open something before it throws. It counts as ready only after onReady succeeds. That is exactly the runtime's rollback.
questions.expected:
shutdown tasks
shutdown store
destroy http
destroy tasks
destroy store
http failed to start

questions.q: Finish runChecks(checks). checks is a Map of name to function (maybe async). Return { ready, health }: ready is true only if every check returns true, and health is "healthy" when ready, otherwise "degraded".
questions.explain: await works on plain values too, so the same loop handles sync and async checks. One failing check makes the app not ready: still alive, but degraded.

questions.q: Finish boot(runtime), like src/server.ts should do: try await runtime.start(). If it throws, print Startup failed: MESSAGE, await runtime.stop(), and return 1. On success return 0. The number is the exit code.
questions.explain: Stop after a failed start to release anything the rollback did not reach, then exit non-zero. Exit code 1 tells the platform the app did not start, so it can restart it or alert you.
questions.expected:
exit code 0
Startup failed: Port 3000 is already in use
stopped
exit code 1

questions.q: Finish stopWithin(stop, ms): wait for stop(), but give up after ms milliseconds. Return "stopped" if it finished in time, else "timed out". Clear the timer either way.
questions.explain: Promise.race settles with whichever finishes first. This is what shutdownTimeout does for you (30 seconds by default): a hanging hook cannot block shutdown forever.
